description: Execute the design control process for a medical device per FDA 21 CFR 820.30 and ISO 13485: capture design inputs from user needs and clinical requirements, perform risk analysis, produce design outputs, verify against specifications, validate in the use environment, and transfer to manufacturing with full traceability.

steps.description: Translate user needs and clinical requirements into measurable design input specifications with acceptance criteria, linking each input to the originating need.

inputs.name: intended-use-statement
inputs.desc: Description of the device's intended use, indications, patient population, and use environment

inputs.name: user-needs-list
inputs.desc: Raw list of user needs gathered from clinicians, patients, and stakeholders

inputs.name: predicate-device-analysis
inputs.desc: Analysis of similar legally marketed devices and their specifications

outputs.name: design-input-specifications
outputs.desc: Measurable requirements with acceptance criteria, each traced to a user need

outputs.name: design-input-traceability
outputs.desc: Matrix linking each design input to its originating user need and applicable standard

process: For each user need, define one or more measurable requirements. A need like 'easy to hold' becomes 'grip force less than 10N for 95th percentile hand' with a specific test method.

Identify applicable standards and extract requirements from them. IEC 60601-1 for electrical safety, ISO 10993 for biocompatibility, IEC 62366 for usability. Each standard clause that applies becomes a design input.
For performance requirements, define acceptance criteria that are testable: a number, a pass/fail condition, or a reference to a standard test method. Avoid subjective language.
Cross-reference predicate device specifications. Any specification you choose that is less stringent than the predicate needs a documented rationale.
Build the traceability matrix: user need to design input to verification method. Every user need must trace to at least one design input. Every design input must have an assigned verification method.

steps.description: Perform risk analysis per ISO 14971: identify hazards, estimate risk, evaluate acceptability, and define risk control measures that feed back into design inputs and verification requirements.

inputs.name: design-input-specifications
inputs.desc: Measurable requirements from design inputs

inputs.name: intended-use-statement
inputs.desc: Device intended use and use environment

outputs.name: risk-management-file
outputs.desc: Hazard analysis, risk estimation, risk evaluation, and risk control measures per ISO 14971

outputs.name: risk-derived-design-inputs
outputs.desc: New design inputs generated from risk control measures that must be added to the specification

outputs.name: residual-risk-assessment
outputs.desc: Assessment of residual risk after controls, with overall risk-benefit determination

process: Identify hazards systematically using the device's intended use and foreseeable misuse. Walk through each use scenario: unpacking, setup, normal use, cleaning, maintenance, disposal. For each, ask what can go wrong.

For each hazard, identify the hazardous situation (exposure pathway) and the harm. Estimate severity from clinical consequence (negligible, minor, serious, critical, catastrophic) and probability from the causal chain (not just frequency of the hazard but likelihood it reaches the patient).

Plot each risk on the risk acceptability matrix. Risks in the unacceptable region require risk control. Risks in the ALARP region require documented justification that further reduction is not practicable.

Design risk controls in priority order: inherent safety by design first (eliminate the hazard), then protective measures in the device (guards, alarms, interlocks), then information for safety (warnings, instructions) last.
For each risk control measure, create a new design input or modify an existing one. The control measure is not real until it appears in the design specification with a verification method.
After all controls are defined, estimate residual risk. Verify no new hazards were introduced by the controls. Document the overall residual risk and the risk-benefit analysis.

steps.description: Produce design outputs that conform to design inputs: device specifications, drawings, software requirements, manufacturing procedures, and acceptance criteria that together define the device completely enough to manufacture and test it.

inputs.name: design-input-specifications
inputs.desc: Complete design inputs including risk-derived requirements

inputs.name: risk-management-file
inputs.desc: Risk controls that must be implemented in the design

inputs.name: risk-derived-design-inputs
inputs.desc: Additional requirements from risk analysis

outputs.name: design-output-package
outputs.desc: Complete set of device specifications, drawings, BOMs, software specs, and manufacturing procedures

outputs.name: acceptance-criteria
outputs.desc: Inspection and test criteria for manufacturing acceptance

outputs.name: design-output-traceability
outputs.desc: Matrix linking each design output to its design input

process: For each design input, produce the design output that satisfies it. A performance requirement becomes a detailed specification with tolerances. A biocompatibility requirement becomes a material specification with grade and supplier qualification.
Generate engineering drawings with GD&T per ASME Y14.5. Every dimension on the drawing must trace to a design input or manufacturing need. Do not tolerance dimensions that do not affect function.
Write software requirements specifications per IEC 62304. Assign software safety class (A, B, or C) from the risk analysis. Class C software requires unit-level verification of every requirement.

Define manufacturing procedures for special processes (welding, bonding, sterilization). Each procedure must include process parameters, equipment calibration requirements, and operator qualification.

Define incoming, in-process, and final acceptance criteria. Each acceptance criterion must trace to a design input. Sampling plans must be justified by process capability data or regulatory requirement.

steps.description: Verify that design outputs meet design inputs through testing, analysis, and inspection. Each design input gets at least one verification activity with documented results.

inputs.name: design-input-specifications
inputs.desc: Requirements to verify against

inputs.name: design-output-package
inputs.desc: The device design to be verified

inputs.name: design-output-traceability
inputs.desc: Which outputs address which inputs

outputs.name: verification-test-reports
outputs.desc: Test reports for each verification activity with pass/fail results and raw data

outputs.name: verification-traceability
outputs.desc: Updated traceability matrix showing verification status for every design input

process: For each design input, select the verification method: test (measure against acceptance criteria), analysis (calculation or simulation with documented assumptions), or inspection (visual or dimensional check). Test is preferred when feasible.

Write test protocols before testing. Each protocol defines the test objective (which design input), test setup, sample size with statistical justification, procedure, acceptance criteria, and data recording forms.

Execute tests on design output samples that are representative of production. Document any deviations from the protocol. If a test fails, do not retest without root cause analysis and documented rationale.
For analysis-based verification, document the analysis method, assumptions, input data, calculations, and conclusion. If the analysis uses simulation (FEA, CFD), document the model validation.

Compile the verification traceability matrix. Every design input must show a completed verification activity with a pass/fail result. Any open item is a design gap that must be resolved before design transfer.

steps.description: Validate the device under actual or simulated use conditions to confirm it meets user needs, then transfer the validated design to manufacturing with complete documentation.

inputs.name: verification-test-reports
inputs.desc: Completed verification results

inputs.name: design-output-package
inputs.desc: Final device design documentation

inputs.name: risk-management-file
inputs.desc: Risk file with residual risk assessment

inputs.name: verification-traceability
inputs.desc: Verification status for all inputs

outputs.name: validation-report
outputs.desc: Results of validation testing under use conditions with clinical or simulated-use data

outputs.name: design-history-file
outputs.desc: Complete DHF containing all design control records from inputs through validation

outputs.name: design-transfer-package
outputs.desc: Manufacturing-ready documentation with device master record, process validations, and acceptance procedures

process: Design validation tests the finished device (or production-equivalent units) under conditions of actual or simulated use. This is not re-verification. It answers: does the device satisfy the user need in the hands of the intended user?

For devices requiring clinical data, design the clinical study per the clinical trial plan. For devices where simulated use suffices, design the simulated-use study with representative users performing representative tasks.
Validation must include software validation (per IEC 62304), usability validation (per IEC 62366), biocompatibility testing (per ISO 10993), and sterilization validation if applicable.

Compile the design history file: user needs, design inputs, risk management file, design outputs, verification results, validation results, and all design review records. This is the regulatory submission evidence.

Execute design transfer: hand off the device master record to manufacturing, confirm that process validations (IQ/OQ/PQ) are complete, verify that incoming/in-process/final inspection procedures are in place, and confirm that trained personnel are available.

description: Plan and execute a biocompatibility evaluation per ISO 10993: classify device contact, select tests, execute chemical characterization and biological testing, and compile the biological evaluation report for regulatory submission.

steps.description: Classify the device by body contact type and duration per ISO 10993-1, then select the required biological tests and chemical characterization studies.

inputs.name: device-description
inputs.desc: Materials, manufacturing processes, sterilization method, and intended use of the device

inputs.name: contact-classification
inputs.desc: Body contact type (surface, external communicating, implant) and duration (limited, prolonged, permanent)

outputs.name: biological-evaluation-plan
outputs.desc: List of required biological tests and chemical characterization studies with rationale for each

outputs.name: material-characterization-plan
outputs.desc: Plan for chemical characterization of extractables and leachables from all patient-contacting materials

process: Classify the device per ISO 10993-1 Table A.1: body contact nature (surface contacting skin, mucosal membrane, breached surface; external communicating blood path, tissue/bone, circulating blood; implant tissue/bone, blood) and duration (limited: under 24h, prolonged: 24h to 30 days, permanent: over 30 days).

From the classification, identify the required biological endpoints per ISO 10993-1 Table A.1: cytotoxicity, sensitization, irritation, acute systemic toxicity, subacute/subchronic/chronic toxicity, genotoxicity, implantation, hemocompatibility, carcinogenicity, reproductive/developmental toxicity.

Evaluate existing data before planning new tests. If the same material with the same processing and sterilization has been tested for another device with equal or greater contact, that data may be leveraged with documented equivalence rationale.

Plan chemical characterization per ISO 10993-18. Identify extraction conditions (solvents, temperature, time) that simulate worst-case clinical use. Polar and non-polar solvents at elevated temperature for exhaustive extraction.

For each biological endpoint without adequate existing data, specify the test standard (ISO 10993-5 for cytotoxicity, ISO 10993-10 for irritation, ISO 10993-11 for systemic toxicity), sample preparation, and test lab requirements.

steps.description: Execute chemical characterization: extract patient-contacting materials under simulated-use and exaggerated conditions, identify and quantify extractables, and perform toxicological risk assessment of each chemical species.

inputs.name: material-characterization-plan
inputs.desc: Extraction conditions and analytical methods

inputs.name: device-description
inputs.desc: Materials, processes, and sterilization affecting extractable profile

outputs.name: extractables-report
outputs.desc: Identified and quantified chemical species from each extraction condition with analytical method validation

outputs.name: toxicological-risk-assessment
outputs.desc: Risk assessment of each extractable species against tolerable intake values, with margin of safety calculation

process: Prepare test articles: final-finished devices or representative material coupons processed and sterilized identically to production. Include negative controls (extraction solvent only) and positive controls where applicable.

Extract in polar (water, saline, or water/ethanol) and non-polar (hexane or similar) solvents. Use elevated temperature (50C or 70C) to simulate accelerated aging. Extraction time based on device contact duration: 72h for permanent implants.

Analyze extracts by GC-MS for volatile and semi-volatile organics, LC-MS for non-volatile organics, ICP-MS or ICP-OES for metals, FTIR for polymer degradation products. Report limits of detection for each method.
Identify each detected species by library matching (NIST, Wiley) and quantify by calibrated standards. For unknowns, assign a toxicological threshold of concern (TTC) per Cramer class.

Calculate tolerable exposure for each identified species using ISO 10993-17. Compare patient exposure (extractable quantity per device, per day) to tolerable intake (TI). Report the margin of safety (TI divided by estimated exposure). Any margin below 1.0 requires risk control.

steps.description: Execute the required biological tests (cytotoxicity, sensitization, irritation, systemic toxicity, genotoxicity, implantation, hemocompatibility) per ISO 10993 test standards and compile results.

inputs.name: biological-evaluation-plan
inputs.desc: Tests to execute with standards and sample prep requirements

inputs.name: extractables-report
inputs.desc: Chemical characterization results informing test design

outputs.name: biological-test-reports
outputs.desc: Individual test reports for each biological endpoint with pass/fail against acceptance criteria

outputs.name: biological-evaluation-report
outputs.desc: Integrated report per ISO 10993-1 summarizing all biological evidence and overall biocompatibility conclusion

process: Cytotoxicity per ISO 10993-5: MEM elution or direct contact method with L-929 cells. Grade reactivity 0-4. Grade 2 or higher is a cytotoxic response requiring investigation. Also run quantitative viability assay (MTT or XTT) reporting percent viability vs negative control.

Sensitization: LLNA (local lymph node assay per ISO 10993-10 Annex B) as first choice due to reduction in animal use. Stimulation index below 3.0 is non-sensitizing. If LLNA is not applicable (device extracts are too viscous or colored), use guinea pig maximization test (GPMT).

Irritation per ISO 10993-10 or ISO 10993-23 (reconstructed human cornea-like epithelium for ocular devices). For skin-contacting devices, intracutaneous reactivity test in rabbits or in-vitro reconstructed skin model.

Genotoxicity per ISO 10993-3: Ames test (bacterial reverse mutation) plus in-vitro mammalian cell assay (mouse lymphoma or chromosomal aberration). Both must be negative. A positive result in either requires follow-up in-vivo test (micronucleus).

For implant devices: implantation test per ISO 10993-6 with histopathological evaluation at specified time points. For blood-contacting devices: hemocompatibility per ISO 10993-4 (hemolysis, thrombosis, coagulation, platelet, complement, hematology as applicable).

Compile the biological evaluation report per ISO 10993-1. Integrate chemical characterization, biological test results, clinical data, and literature review. State the overall biocompatibility conclusion with any conditions or limitations.

description: Design an implantable electronic device: hermetic packaging, feedthroughs, power source, ultra-low-power circuits, wireless telemetry, and antenna design within tissue, with longevity and sterilization qualification.

steps.description: Design the hermetic enclosure for implantable electronics: material selection, sealing method, feedthrough design, and hermeticity testing methodology.

inputs.name: device-functional-requirements
inputs.desc: Size constraints, number of electrical feedthroughs, internal volume needed, mechanical loads

inputs.name: implant-environment
inputs.desc: Body location, tissue interface, expected lifetime, temperature and mechanical loading

outputs.name: enclosure-design
outputs.desc: Material, geometry, wall thickness, sealing method, and feedthrough specifications

outputs.name: hermeticity-specification
outputs.desc: Leak rate requirement and test methodology (helium fine leak, gross leak)

process: Select enclosure material: titanium (Grade 1, 2, or 23) is the default for long-term implants due to biocompatibility and weldability. Ceramic (alumina, zirconia) for RF-transparent windows. Titanium wall thickness typically 0.25 to 0.5mm for structural integrity during laser welding.

Design feedthroughs for electrical connections: glass-to-metal seal (alumina ceramic with platinum or niobium pins brazed with gold) is standard. Ceramic-to-metal brazed feedthroughs for higher pin counts. Each pin must maintain hermeticity after thermal cycling (-40C to +60C, 1000 cycles minimum).

Specify the sealing method: laser welding for titanium lids (pulsed Nd:YAG or fiber laser, seam weld, 100% overlap). Weld parameters must produce full-penetration without internal spatter. Weld cross-section metallography on process qualification samples.

Set hermeticity requirement: fine leak rate below 1e-9 atm-cc/sec helium for active implants with multi-year lifetime. This corresponds to moisture ingress below the threshold that corrodes wire bonds over the device lifetime. Test per MIL-STD-883 Method 1014.

Account for internal moisture: desiccant or getter inside the enclosure to absorb residual moisture from assembly. Seal in dry nitrogen or argon. Calculate moisture budget: initial moisture from outgassing + ingress over lifetime must stay below the corrosion threshold for aluminum bond pads.

steps.description: Design the power source and wireless communication system for an implantable device: battery selection or wireless power transfer, ultra-low-power circuit design, and RF telemetry through tissue.

inputs.name: enclosure-design
inputs.desc: Available internal volume and feedthrough count

inputs.name: device-functional-requirements
inputs.desc: Power budget, data rate, communication range, and expected device lifetime

outputs.name: power-system-design
outputs.desc: Battery selection or wireless power transfer design with lifetime analysis

outputs.name: telemetry-system-design
outputs.desc: RF link design with antenna, frequency, modulation, and SAR compliance

outputs.name: ultra-low-power-architecture
outputs.desc: Circuit architecture with power budget allocation across subsystems

process: Power source selection: primary lithium battery (Li/CFx or Li/SOCl2 for high energy density, 10+ year shelf life) for sealed devices like pacemakers. Rechargeable lithium-ion for higher-power devices (neurostimulators) with inductive wireless charging. Battery volume is typically 40-60% of implant volume.

For rechargeable systems, design the inductive wireless power link: primary coil (external) and secondary coil (implanted). Operating frequency 100-500kHz for charging (lower tissue absorption). Link efficiency depends on coil alignment, coupling coefficient, and tissue gap. Design for the worst-case alignment with sufficient margin.

Allocate the power budget across subsystems: sensing (typically microamp range), signal processing (depends on algorithm complexity, target sub-milliamp with duty cycling), stimulation if applicable (dominates budget in neurostimulators), and telemetry (burst transmission to minimize average power). Total average current target: sub-10uA for decade-lifetime battery devices.

Design the RF telemetry link: MICS band (402-405 MHz, dedicated for implants) or ISM 2.4GHz. Antenna design accounts for tissue loading (dielectric constant ~50 for muscle at 400MHz reduces antenna effective size). Meandered dipole or loop antenna on a ceramic substrate inside or on the enclosure. SAR must comply with IEC 62209.

Circuit architecture: microcontroller with deep-sleep modes (sub-100nA sleep current), wake-on-event, and burst processing. ADC with auto-ranging. Telemetry IC with protocol stack in hardware. Eliminate all pull-up resistors and leakage paths. Use voltage regulators with sub-1uA quiescent current.

steps.description: Qualify the implantable device for the intended lifetime through accelerated aging, hermeticity monitoring, and reliability testing specific to the implant environment.

inputs.name: enclosure-design
inputs.desc: Hermetic package with feedthroughs and seal

inputs.name: power-system-design
inputs.desc: Battery or power transfer system with lifetime projection

inputs.name: telemetry-system-design
inputs.desc: RF link and antenna design

outputs.name: longevity-qualification-report
outputs.desc: Results of accelerated aging, hermeticity, corrosion, and reliability testing with projected device lifetime

outputs.name: sterilization-compatibility-report
outputs.desc: Validation that sterilization method does not degrade device performance or hermeticity

process: Accelerated aging: immerse sealed devices in saline at 67C (acceleration factor ~10x at Q10=2 per ASTM F1980) for a duration corresponding to the intended lifetime. Monitor hermeticity (fine leak test at intervals), electrical function, and battery voltage over the aging period.

Corrosion testing: polarization scans on enclosure materials in simulated body fluid (SBF per ISO 23317 or Ringer's solution). Measure corrosion potential, breakdown potential, and repassivation potential. Titanium should show no pitting up to 1V vs SCE in chloride-containing solutions.

Feedthrough reliability: thermal cycle feedthroughs (-40C to +85C, 1000 cycles per IEC 60068-2-14) and test hermeticity after cycling. Pull-test feedthrough pins to verify braze joint integrity. Electrical insulation resistance between pins must remain above 100 megohms.

Sterilization compatibility: process devices through the intended sterilization method (EtO or gamma) and verify no change in hermeticity, electrical performance, or battery capacity. For gamma, test at the maximum validated dose (typically 50kGy for qualification at 25kGy sterilization dose) to account for dose non-uniformity.

Compile longevity report with projected failure rate and lifetime using Weibull analysis of accelerated test data. Apply appropriate acceleration factor derating. Report any failure mechanisms observed and their mitigation in the final design.

description: Design a controlled drug delivery system: select release mechanism, design formulation or device, model pharmacokinetics, and validate release profile through in-vitro and stability testing.

steps.description: Select the drug release mechanism and delivery platform based on the therapeutic target, drug properties, and clinical requirements.

inputs.name: drug-properties
inputs.desc: Molecular weight, solubility, stability, therapeutic window, half-life, and required dosing duration

inputs.name: clinical-requirements
inputs.desc: Target tissue, route of administration, desired release profile (constant, pulsatile, triggered), and treatment duration

outputs.name: delivery-platform-selection
outputs.desc: Selected delivery system type with rationale (polymer matrix, reservoir, osmotic pump, microparticle, implant, transdermal)

outputs.name: target-release-profile
outputs.desc: Quantitative release rate vs time specification with therapeutic window bounds

process: Map drug properties to feasible delivery platforms. Low molecular weight, lipophilic drugs suit transdermal or matrix systems. Peptides and proteins need protection from degradation, pointing toward encapsulation or reservoir systems. Long-duration (months) favors implants; days to weeks favors microparticles or osmotic pumps.

Define the target release profile from pharmacokinetic requirements. Zero-order (constant rate) maintains steady-state plasma levels within the therapeutic window. First-order gives an initial burst then decline. Pulsatile mimics natural secretion patterns.

For polymer-based systems, select the polymer: PLGA for biodegradable depot lasting weeks to months (tune degradation by lactide:glycolide ratio and molecular weight). EVA or silicone for non-degradable implants requiring surgical removal. PEG-based hydrogels for tissue-compatible in-situ forming depots.

For each candidate platform, estimate the feasibility: can it contain the required drug mass, achieve the target rate, survive the sterilization method, and remain stable during shelf life? Eliminate infeasible options before committing to development.

Select the primary platform and define a backup. Document the selection rationale including the risk of each option. The backup matters because formulation development frequently encounters unexpected drug-polymer interactions.

steps.description: Develop the drug delivery formulation or device: polymer processing, drug loading, and in-vitro release testing to match the target release profile.

inputs.name: delivery-platform-selection
inputs.desc: Selected platform and polymer system

inputs.name: target-release-profile
inputs.desc: Quantitative release specification

inputs.name: drug-properties
inputs.desc: Drug characteristics affecting formulation

outputs.name: formulation-specification
outputs.desc: Composition, processing parameters, drug loading, and dimensional specifications

outputs.name: in-vitro-release-data
outputs.desc: Measured release profile from dissolution testing with comparison to target

process: For PLGA microparticles: select encapsulation method (double emulsion W/O/W for hydrophilic drugs, single emulsion O/W for hydrophobic). Process variables: polymer concentration, emulsification speed, surfactant type and concentration, solvent system. Each variable affects particle size, encapsulation efficiency, and burst release.

For matrix implants: mix drug with polymer at the target loading (typically 10-40% w/w). Process by hot-melt extrusion or compression molding. Drug distribution uniformity is critical: verify by sectioning and assaying at multiple locations. Non-uniform loading produces non-uniform release.

For reservoir systems: fabricate the membrane with controlled thickness and porosity. Membrane permeability determines release rate. Rate = (permeability * area * concentration gradient) / membrane thickness. Measure membrane permeability independently before assembling the full device.

Run in-vitro dissolution testing per USP Apparatus 4 (flow-through cell) or appropriate method. Use biorelevant media (pH 7.4 PBS with surfactant if needed for drug solubility). Temperature at 37C. Sample at intervals and assay by HPLC. Compare measured release to target profile.

Iterate formulation parameters to match the target. If burst release is too high, increase polymer molecular weight or add a barrier coating. If release is too slow, increase drug loading, decrease particle size, or switch to a faster-degrading polymer grade. Document each iteration.

steps.description: Model pharmacokinetics from the in-vitro release data to predict in-vivo plasma levels, then execute stability testing to establish shelf life.

inputs.name: in-vitro-release-data
inputs.desc: Measured release profile from dissolution

inputs.name: formulation-specification
inputs.desc: Final formulation composition and dimensions

inputs.name: drug-properties
inputs.desc: Pharmacokinetic parameters (clearance, volume of distribution, bioavailability)

outputs.name: pk-model-predictions
outputs.desc: Predicted plasma concentration vs time with therapeutic window overlay

outputs.name: stability-data
outputs.desc: Stability results at accelerated and long-term conditions with shelf-life determination

outputs.name: release-specification
outputs.desc: Final release specification with acceptance criteria for manufacturing QC

process: Build a compartmental PK model: one- or two-compartment depending on drug distribution. Input the in-vitro release rate as the absorption rate (with in-vitro/in-vivo correlation if available from prior formulations of the same drug). Simulate plasma concentration over the dosing interval.

Compare predicted plasma levels to the therapeutic window. If Cmax exceeds the toxic threshold, reduce burst release. If Cmin falls below the effective concentration before the next dose, increase the sustained release rate or shorten the dosing interval.

For long-acting injectables, apply an IVIVC (in-vitro/in-vivo correlation) level A if possible: point-to-point relationship between in-vitro dissolution and in-vivo absorption. This allows in-vitro release to serve as a surrogate for bioequivalence in future formulation changes.

Execute stability studies per ICH Q1A: long-term (25C/60%RH), accelerated (40C/75%RH), and intermediate if needed. Test at 0, 3, 6, 9, 12 months minimum. Measure drug content, degradation products, release profile, and appearance at each time point.

Determine shelf life from stability data: the time point at which the release profile first exceeds the specification limits at the long-term condition, with statistical analysis per ICH Q1E. The accelerated condition data supports interim shelf life claims while long-term data accumulates.

description: Design and validate a diagnostic assay: select architecture, optimize analytical performance, establish limit of detection, validate precision and accuracy, and prepare for regulatory submission.

steps.description: Select the assay platform, capture reagent, and detection method based on the target analyte, required sensitivity, and clinical use case.

inputs.name: target-analyte
inputs.desc: The biomarker or pathogen to detect: molecular identity, expected concentration range in clinical samples, sample matrix

inputs.name: clinical-use-case
inputs.desc: Point-of-care vs central lab, quantitative vs qualitative, turnaround time requirement, throughput

outputs.name: assay-architecture
outputs.desc: Selected platform (lateral flow, ELISA, PCR, electrochemical), detection method, and capture reagent strategy

outputs.name: performance-targets
outputs.desc: Target sensitivity, specificity, precision, and limit of detection based on clinical decision points

process: Match analyte concentration to detection technology sensitivity. Lateral flow immunoassay detects ng/mL range (adequate for hCG, cardiac troponin triage). ELISA reaches pg/mL (cytokines, tumor markers). PCR detects single copies of nucleic acid (infectious disease, genetic mutations). Electrochemical sensors suit continuous monitoring (glucose).

For immunoassays, select the capture reagent: monoclonal antibody for high specificity, polyclonal for broader epitope recognition, aptamer for chemical stability and batch consistency. Sandwich format (two antibodies) for larger analytes with multiple epitopes. Competitive format for small molecules with single epitopes.

For nucleic acid tests, select the amplification method: real-time PCR for quantitative detection in a lab, isothermal amplification (LAMP, RPA) for point-of-care simplicity (no thermal cycler). Design primers and probes targeting conserved regions of the pathogen genome to avoid false negatives from mutations.

Define performance targets from the clinical decision point. If the clinical cutoff is 0.04 ng/mL (high-sensitivity troponin), the assay LoD must be well below that, and precision at the cutoff must yield a CV below 10%. Total imprecision determines whether the assay can distinguish clinically meaningful changes.

Select the detection method: colorimetric (visual read for qualitative, reader for quantitative), fluorescent (higher sensitivity, requires reader), chemiluminescent (highest sensitivity for immunoassay, lab-based), electrochemical (direct transduction, suitable for miniaturization and continuous sensing).

steps.description: Optimize assay conditions for maximum signal-to-noise, then determine the limit of detection and limit of quantification using CLSI protocols.

inputs.name: assay-architecture
inputs.desc: Platform, reagents, and detection method

inputs.name: performance-targets
inputs.desc: Required sensitivity and precision

outputs.name: optimized-assay-protocol
outputs.desc: Final assay conditions: reagent concentrations, incubation times, temperatures, wash steps

outputs.name: lod-loq-determination
outputs.desc: Limit of detection and limit of quantification with confidence intervals and blank study data

process: Optimize sequentially: antibody/primer concentration first (checkerboard titration for sandwich immunoassay), then incubation time, then blocking agent, then wash stringency. At each step, measure both signal (positive control) and noise (negative control). Maximize the signal-to-noise ratio, not just signal.

For immunoassays, optimize blocking to reduce nonspecific binding: test BSA, casein, fish gelatin, and proprietary blockers. Measure background signal on each. The blocker that produces the lowest background at the negative control is the winner, even if it slightly reduces positive signal.
Determine limit of blank (LoB) per CLSI EP17: measure 60+ blank replicates across 3+ days. LoB = mean blank + 1.645 * SD blank (for 95% confidence that a blank will not exceed this value).

Determine limit of detection (LoD): measure 60+ replicates of low-concentration samples (near expected LoD) across 3+ days. LoD = LoB + 1.645 * SD of the low-concentration sample. This gives 95% confidence of detecting a true positive at the LoD concentration.

Determine limit of quantification (LoQ): the lowest concentration at which the assay meets the required precision target (typically CV below 20% or below 10% depending on clinical need). Measure precision at multiple low concentrations and identify the concentration where the CV requirement is met.

steps.description: Validate assay precision, accuracy, linearity, interference, and clinical performance, then compile the analytical and clinical validation package for regulatory submission.

inputs.name: optimized-assay-protocol
inputs.desc: Final assay conditions

inputs.name: lod-loq-determination
inputs.desc: Sensitivity characterization

inputs.name: performance-targets
inputs.desc: Required analytical and clinical performance

outputs.name: analytical-validation-report
outputs.desc: Precision, accuracy, linearity, interference, and carryover study results

outputs.name: clinical-validation-report
outputs.desc: Clinical sensitivity and specificity vs reference method from clinical specimens

outputs.name: regulatory-submission-package
outputs.desc: Complete analytical and clinical evidence package for 510(k), De Novo, or PMA submission

process: Precision study per CLSI EP05: 2 levels (normal and abnormal), 2 runs per day, 2 replicates per run, 20 days. Calculate within-run, between-run, between-day, and total imprecision. Report as CV at each level. Compare to performance targets.

Method comparison per CLSI EP09: test 40+ clinical specimens spanning the reportable range against the reference method. Analyze by Passing-Bablok regression (slope and intercept with 95% CI) and Bland-Altman difference plot (bias and limits of agreement). Acceptable bias depends on clinical use.

Linearity per CLSI EP06: prepare mixtures of high and low patient pools at 5+ levels spanning the claimed range. Run in triplicate. Perform polynomial regression; if first-order (linear) fits within allowable error, the range is verified. If non-linear, restrict the reportable range.

Interference testing per CLSI EP07: test common endogenous interferents (hemoglobin, bilirubin, lipemia, biotin) and relevant exogenous substances (common medications) at concentrations encountered in clinical specimens. Report bias at each interferent concentration.

Clinical validation: test 100+ clinical specimens with known disease status (confirmed by clinical diagnosis or reference standard). Calculate clinical sensitivity (true positive rate) and clinical specificity (true negative rate) with 95% confidence intervals. For 510(k), demonstrate substantial equivalence to predicate device performance.

description: Select, develop, and validate a sterilization process for a medical device: method selection, bioburden characterization, cycle development, dose setting or cycle qualification, and ongoing sterility assurance.

steps.description: Select the sterilization method based on device materials, design, and performance requirements, with material compatibility testing.

inputs.name: device-materials-list
inputs.desc: All materials in the device with thermal, chemical, and radiation sensitivity data

inputs.name: device-design-characteristics
inputs.desc: Geometry, packaging, electronics presence, moisture sensitivity

outputs.name: sterilization-method
outputs.desc: Selected method (EtO, gamma, e-beam, steam, VHP) with rationale and material compatibility evidence

outputs.name: material-compatibility-data
outputs.desc: Test results showing device performance after sterilization exposure at qualification dose

process: Screen methods by material compatibility: gamma and e-beam cause chain scission in PTFE, UHMWPE, and some polymers (cross-linking in others). EtO requires gas permeation through packaging and residual limits. Steam requires heat tolerance above 121C. VHP requires oxidation tolerance. Electronics generally exclude steam and may have radiation dose limits.

For each candidate method, expose material coupons or test articles to the qualification-level dose (typically 1.5x to 2x the sterilization dose for radiation, or a multi-cycle exposure for EtO). Test mechanical properties, dimensional stability, color change, and device functionality after exposure.

For radiation sterilization, determine the dose window: minimum dose for sterility (25kGy is the standard starting point, VDmax method per ISO 11137-2 can qualify a lower dose), maximum dose limited by material degradation. If the window is too narrow, radiation is not suitable.

For EtO, verify gas penetration: package the device as intended and run a fractional cycle. Place biological indicators (Bacillus atrophaeus spore strips) at the most difficult-to-reach locations. If BIs survive, redesign packaging or device access for gas penetration.
Document the selection rationale, referencing material compatibility data, and identify the applicable standard: ISO 11135 for EtO, ISO 11137 for radiation, ISO 17665 for steam, ISO 22441 for VHP.

steps.description: Develop and validate the sterilization cycle: bioburden characterization, dose setting or cycle parameter qualification, and performance qualification with biological indicators.

inputs.name: sterilization-method
inputs.desc: Selected method with applicable standard

inputs.name: device-design-characteristics
inputs.desc: Device and packaging configuration for sterilization

outputs.name: bioburden-characterization
outputs.desc: Bioburden count and identification on production-representative devices

outputs.name: validated-sterilization-cycle
outputs.desc: Qualified cycle parameters with biological indicator and dosimetric evidence of sterility assurance level 10^-6

process: Determine product bioburden per ISO 11737-1: test 10+ production units from at least 3 production lots. Use membrane filtration or direct immersion culture. Report average bioburden count and identify predominant organisms. Bioburden data drives the dose or cycle severity needed.

For radiation (ISO 11137-2): use VDmax method for low bioburden products (under 1000 CFU). Irradiate 10 product items at the verification dose. If no more than 1 of 10 is positive for growth, the 25kGy substantiation dose is validated. For higher bioburden, use Method 1 or 2 with augmented bioburden.

For EtO (ISO 11135): develop the cycle in three phases. First, determine the minimum cycle parameters through fractional cycle studies with BIs at worst-case locations. Then run half-cycles to confirm BI inactivation approach. Finally, run full cycles with product load configurations representing worst case (maximum load density, hardest-to-sterilize orientation).

Performance qualification: run 3 consecutive sterilization cycles under worst-case conditions (minimum gas concentration, minimum time, coldest temperature for EtO; minimum dose for radiation). All BIs must be inactivated (for EtO). Dosimeters must confirm minimum dose delivery at the minimum-dose location (for radiation).

Establish routine monitoring: dosimetric release for radiation (every load), BI and chemical indicator monitoring for EtO (every load), bioburden trending (quarterly). Define revalidation triggers: change in product design, packaging, bioburden, or sterilization equipment.

description: Apply the usability engineering process for medical devices per IEC 62366-1 and FDA human factors guidance: use-related risk analysis, formative evaluation, and summative validation to demonstrate safe and effective use.

steps.description: Identify use-related hazards through task analysis and use-error prediction, linking use risks to the risk management file per ISO 14971.

inputs.name: intended-use-and-users
inputs.desc: Device intended use, user profiles (professional, lay user, patient), and use environments

inputs.name: device-user-interface
inputs.desc: Description of all user interface elements: controls, displays, labels, alarms, connections, accessories

outputs.name: use-specification
outputs.desc: User profiles, use environments, and task analysis for all use scenarios

outputs.name: use-related-risk-analysis
outputs.desc: Identified use errors, their root causes (perception, cognition, action), associated hazards, and risk priority

process: Define user profiles: training level, physical capabilities (vision, dexterity, strength), experience with similar devices, cognitive state during use (emergency department stress vs routine clinic). Each profile may interact differently with the same interface.

Conduct task analysis: break each use scenario (setup, use, maintenance, disposal) into sequential tasks. For each task, identify the information the user needs, the action they must take, and the feedback they receive. This reveals the user-device interaction at each step.

For each task, predict possible use errors: perception errors (did not see the alarm, misread the display), cognitive errors (misinterpreted the reading, selected wrong mode), and action errors (pressed wrong button, connected wrong port, applied wrong force). Predict based on known human factors principles, not assumptions about careful users.

Link each predicted use error to its consequence (hazard and harm) and estimate risk. High-severity use errors (wrong drug, wrong dose, wrong patient) drive the design priority. Use errors that are common but low-severity may be acceptable with information for safety.

Prioritize use-related risks and define risk control measures. Design controls first (make the error impossible or self-correcting), then protective controls (interlocks, alarms), then training and labeling last. Each control measure must be verifiable through usability testing.

steps.description: Conduct formative usability studies during design to identify and fix usability problems before the design is finalized.

inputs.name: use-related-risk-analysis
inputs.desc: Identified use errors and risk controls to evaluate

inputs.name: device-user-interface
inputs.desc: Current prototype or mockup of the user interface

outputs.name: formative-findings
outputs.desc: Usability problems identified, root causes, severity, and design recommendations

outputs.name: design-iterations
outputs.desc: Interface modifications made in response to formative findings

process: Plan formative studies early and iterate. Five to eight representative users per round is sufficient to identify major usability problems (Nielsen's research shows 5 users find ~85% of problems). Run multiple rounds as the design evolves.

Use think-aloud protocol: ask participants to verbalize their thoughts while performing tasks with the prototype. Observe without coaching. Record task completion success, errors, hesitations, and participant comments. Difficulty is data.

After each round, categorize findings by root cause: is this a perception problem (display too dim, label too small), cognition problem (ambiguous terminology, non-intuitive workflow), or action problem (control too close to another, force too high)? The root cause determines the fix.

For critical tasks (identified from risk analysis), track whether the design change actually prevented the use error. If a user still makes the error after the redesign, the fix did not work. Iterate until the critical-task error rate reaches an acceptable level.

Document formative findings and design iterations in the usability engineering file. Formative studies are not pass/fail. Their purpose is to improve the design. The summative validation study provides the pass/fail evidence.

steps.description: Conduct the summative human factors validation study to demonstrate that the final device can be used safely and effectively by the intended users in the intended environment.

inputs.name: formative-findings
inputs.desc: History of usability problems found and resolved

inputs.name: design-iterations
inputs.desc: Final interface design incorporating formative learnings

inputs.name: use-related-risk-analysis
inputs.desc: Final risk analysis with critical tasks identified

outputs.name: summative-validation-report
outputs.desc: Task completion data, use error data, root cause analysis for any residual use errors, and overall pass/fail determination

outputs.name: usability-engineering-file
outputs.desc: Complete human factors file for regulatory submission

process: Design the summative study: 15 representative users per user group (minimum per FDA guidance). Use the final or production-equivalent device in a simulated use environment that replicates the clinical setting. Include the final labeling (IFU, quick start guide).

Define critical tasks from the risk analysis: tasks where a use error could cause serious harm. Each critical task must be tested. Define the success criteria before testing: what constitutes a successful completion, a use error, and a close call.

Conduct simulated-use sessions: present participants with clinical scenarios requiring them to perform each critical task. Do not train beyond what the intended user would receive. Observe and record task performance, errors, and difficulties. Do not intervene during the task.

After each session, conduct a knowledge-task interview: ask the participant to explain the meaning of displays, symbols, and labels. This tests whether the user understands the information the interface presents, not just whether they can operate the device mechanically.

Analyze results: for each critical task, report the number of successful completions, use errors, and close calls. For each use error, perform root cause analysis (perception, cognition, action). If use errors on critical tasks occurred, assess whether the residual risk is acceptable. No use errors on critical tasks that could cause serious harm is the FDA expectation for summative validation.

description: Design and verify electrical safety for a medical device per IEC 60601-1: classification, insulation design, leakage current management, EMC compliance, and essential performance verification.

steps.description: Classify the device and design the insulation system: MOPP/MOOP determination, creepage and clearance, and protective earth requirements.

inputs.name: device-electrical-architecture
inputs.desc: Power supply topology, patient connections, operator interface, signal paths

inputs.name: applied-parts-definition
inputs.desc: Parts of the device intended to contact the patient, and the type of contact (surface, invasive, cardiac)

outputs.name: safety-classification
outputs.desc: Protection class (I or II), applied part type (B, BF, CF), and insulation diagram showing MOPP and MOOP requirements

outputs.name: insulation-design-specification
outputs.desc: Creepage, clearance, and dielectric withstand requirements for each insulation barrier

process: Classify applied parts: Type B (no direct patient connection or connection that is not critical), Type BF (direct patient connection, floating), Type CF (direct cardiac connection, floating). CF requires the highest level of protection against leakage current through the patient connection.

Determine means of protection: MOPP (means of operator protection) and MOOP (means of patient protection). Between mains and the patient-connected circuit of a CF applied part, 2 MOPP are required. Between mains and the enclosure, 1 MOOP for Class I (with protective earth) or 2 MOOP for Class II (double insulation).

For each insulation barrier, determine creepage and clearance from IEC 60601-1 Table 11 and Table 13. Values depend on working voltage (peak and RMS), pollution degree (typically PD2 for medical devices), and material group (I, II, IIIa, IIIb based on CTI of the insulating material).

Design the dielectric withstand: each MOPP must withstand the test voltage from IEC 60601-1 Table 6 (typically 1500Vrms for mains-rated MOPP, 4000Vrms for reinforced/double insulation). Design PCB spacing and transformer construction to pass this test with margin.

For Class I devices, design the protective earth connection: low-impedance path from accessible conductive parts to the earth terminal. Resistance below 0.1 ohms at 25A for 10 seconds per IEC 60601-1 clause 8.6.4.

steps.description: Verify leakage current limits, design for EMC compliance per IEC 60601-1-2, and verify essential performance is maintained under electromagnetic disturbance.

inputs.name: safety-classification
inputs.desc: Applied part types and protection class

inputs.name: insulation-design-specification
inputs.desc: Insulation barriers and earth path design

inputs.name: device-electrical-architecture
inputs.desc: Circuit topology and signal paths

outputs.name: leakage-current-test-results
outputs.desc: Earth leakage, enclosure leakage, and patient leakage current measurements under normal and single-fault conditions

outputs.name: emc-test-plan-and-results
outputs.desc: EMC emissions and immunity test results per IEC 60601-1-2 with essential performance verification

outputs.name: essential-performance-definition
outputs.desc: Defined essential performance parameters and their acceptance criteria under fault and disturbance conditions

process: Define essential performance: the clinical function that, if degraded, would create an unacceptable risk. For an infusion pump, essential performance is accurate flow rate. For a monitor, it is accurate physiological measurement. Essential performance must be maintained under single-fault and during electromagnetic disturbance.

Measure leakage currents per IEC 60601-1 clause 8.7: earth leakage (normal: 5mA max, single-fault: 10mA), enclosure leakage (normal: 100uA for Type BF, single-fault: 500uA), patient leakage (normal: 10uA for CF, 100uA for BF; single-fault: 50uA for CF, 500uA for BF). Measure in normal condition, open earth, and open neutral.

Design for EMC emissions: conducted emissions below IEC 60601-1-2 limits (Group 1 Class A or B depending on intended environment). Radiated emissions below limits. For professional healthcare environment, Class A limits apply. For home healthcare, Class B (more restrictive).

Design for EMC immunity per IEC 60601-1-2 Table 9: ESD (6kV contact, 8kV air), radiated immunity (3V/m or 10V/m depending on environment and frequency), EFT (1kV on mains), surge (1kV differential, 2kV common mode), conducted immunity, power frequency magnetic field. At each test, verify essential performance is maintained.

Run pre-compliance testing in-house before formal lab testing. Use ESD gun on all accessible surfaces and connections. Use near-field probes to identify emission sources. Fix issues at the design stage: adding ESD protection diodes, improving grounding, adding filtering, and shielding where needed.

description: Design and execute a clinical trial for a medical device: regulatory pathway determination, study design, endpoint selection, enrollment, data analysis, and submission preparation.

steps.description: Determine the regulatory pathway and design the clinical study: IDE determination, study type, endpoints, sample size, and statistical analysis plan.

inputs.name: device-classification
inputs.desc: FDA classification, predicate device (if 510(k)), or novel device rationale (De Novo or PMA)

inputs.name: clinical-evidence-requirements
inputs.desc: What clinical data FDA expects for the submission pathway, from pre-submission feedback or guidance documents

outputs.name: clinical-study-protocol
outputs.desc: Study design, endpoints, sample size, inclusion/exclusion criteria, and statistical analysis plan

outputs.name: ide-application
outputs.desc: IDE application (if significant risk) or abbreviated IDE documentation (if non-significant risk)

process: Determine if the study requires an IDE (Investigational Device Exemption). Significant risk devices (implants, life-sustaining, critical diagnostic) need FDA IDE approval before starting. Non-significant risk devices need IRB approval only. The sponsor makes the initial SR/NSR determination; FDA adjudicates if challenged.

Select the study design. Randomized controlled trial is the standard for PMA. For 510(k) with clinical data, a single-arm study with comparison to published literature or objective performance criteria (OPC) may suffice. Adaptive designs (with pre-specified interim analyses) can reduce enrollment if the effect is larger than expected.

Define primary endpoints: safety endpoint (adverse event rate, typically 6 or 12 months) and effectiveness endpoint (clinical outcome measure relevant to the intended use). The effectiveness endpoint must be clinically meaningful, not just a surrogate. Select validated instruments or outcome measures accepted in the therapeutic area.

Calculate sample size: specify the expected effect size, significance level (alpha, typically 0.05), power (typically 80% or 90%), and expected dropout rate. For superiority trials, the effect size is the minimum clinically important difference. For non-inferiority trials, specify the non-inferiority margin with clinical justification.

Write the statistical analysis plan before enrollment begins. Pre-specify the primary analysis population (ITT, per-protocol), the statistical test, handling of missing data, and the analysis of secondary endpoints. Pre-specification prevents post-hoc statistical fishing.

steps.description: Execute the clinical trial, manage data, analyze results, and compile the clinical evidence package for regulatory submission.

inputs.name: clinical-study-protocol
inputs.desc: Approved study protocol with endpoints and analysis plan

inputs.name: ide-application
inputs.desc: IDE approval (if required) and IRB approvals

outputs.name: clinical-study-report
outputs.desc: Final clinical study report with safety and effectiveness results

outputs.name: regulatory-submission-clinical-section
outputs.desc: Clinical evidence section formatted for 510(k), De Novo, or PMA submission

process: Select and qualify clinical sites: sites must have the patient population, investigator expertise, and infrastructure (IRB, regulatory experience, data management). Conduct site initiation visits to train investigators on the protocol, device, and data collection.

Manage enrollment: track screening, enrollment, and follow-up rates at each site. If enrollment is slower than projected, identify barriers (restrictive inclusion criteria, competing studies, site capacity) and address them. Do not change the protocol to ease enrollment without FDA notification.

Monitor data quality: use a clinical data management system with edit checks. Conduct source data verification at sites (compare CRFs to medical records). Identify and resolve data queries promptly. An independent data monitoring committee (IDMC) reviews safety data at pre-specified intervals for serious adverse events.

Manage adverse event reporting: report unanticipated adverse device effects (UADE) to FDA, all IRBs, and investigators within 10 working days. Report device-related deaths within 10 working days per 21 CFR 812.150. Maintain the adverse event log throughout the study.

Analyze per the pre-specified statistical analysis plan. Report the primary endpoint result with point estimate and confidence interval. Present all adverse events in tabular form with rates and relationship to device. Compile the clinical study report per MEDDEV 2.7/1 or FDA format, and prepare the clinical section of the regulatory submission.

description: Establish and maintain a medical device manufacturing quality system per ISO 13485 and 21 CFR 820: process validation, inspection methods, supplier controls, CAPA, and post-market surveillance.

steps.description: Establish the quality management system: document structure, process definition, resource requirements, and management responsibility per ISO 13485.

inputs.name: device-master-record
inputs.desc: Complete device specifications, drawings, BOMs, and manufacturing procedures from design transfer

inputs.name: regulatory-requirements
inputs.desc: Applicable quality system regulations (21 CFR 820, ISO 13485, EU MDR Annex IX)

outputs.name: quality-manual
outputs.desc: Quality policy, organizational structure, process map, and document control system

outputs.name: process-validation-plan
outputs.desc: List of manufacturing processes requiring validation with IQ/OQ/PQ protocol outlines

process: Define the quality policy and quality objectives. The policy is a statement of commitment to regulatory compliance and continual improvement. Quality objectives must be measurable: defect rate targets, CAPA closure time, audit findings trend.

Map the manufacturing processes: incoming inspection, assembly/fabrication steps, in-process inspection, final inspection, packaging, labeling, sterilization, storage, and distribution. For each process, assign an owner, define inputs and outputs, and identify process controls.

Establish the document control system: procedures, work instructions, forms, and records. Every document must have a unique identifier, revision level, approval signature, and effective date. Changes require documented change orders with impact assessment.

Identify processes that require validation (where the output cannot be fully verified by subsequent inspection or test). Welding, bonding, sealing, sterilization, and software are typically special processes requiring IQ (equipment qualified), OQ (process operates within parameters), and PQ (process consistently produces conforming product).

Define infrastructure and work environment requirements: cleanroom classification (ISO 14644, typically ISO 7 or 8 for medical device assembly), environmental monitoring (particle counts, temperature, humidity), personnel training and gowning, and equipment calibration program.

steps.description: Execute process validation for manufacturing: installation qualification, operational qualification, and performance qualification for each special process.

inputs.name: process-validation-plan
inputs.desc: Processes to validate with protocol outlines

inputs.name: device-master-record
inputs.desc: Process specifications and acceptance criteria

outputs.name: process-validation-reports
outputs.desc: IQ/OQ/PQ reports for each validated process with data and conclusions

outputs.name: control-plan
outputs.desc: Manufacturing control plan specifying in-process controls, inspection points, and sampling plans for each operation

process: Installation Qualification (IQ): verify that equipment is installed per manufacturer specifications. Document equipment make, model, serial number, calibration status, utility connections, and software version. Verify against the purchase specification.

Operational Qualification (OQ): demonstrate that the process operates within specified parameters across the operating range. Identify worst-case parameter combinations (highest and lowest settings that could occur in production). Run the process at worst-case corners and verify output meets acceptance criteria.

Performance Qualification (PQ): run the process at nominal production conditions for 3 consecutive production-sized batches (or 30 consecutive units minimum). Inspect every unit against all acceptance criteria. Calculate process capability (Cpk) for measurable characteristics. Cpk above 1.33 indicates a capable process.

For processes with attribute outputs (pass/fail), use a sampling plan per ANSI/ASQ Z1.4 or demonstrate zero defects in an appropriate sample size for the target defect rate (e.g., 59 units for 95% confidence that the defect rate is below 5%).

Establish the ongoing control plan: specify the process parameter monitoring (frequency, method, limits), in-process inspection points, sampling plans for each inspection, and reaction plans for out-of-specification results. The control plan is the living document that maintains validated state.

steps.description: Operate the CAPA system and post-market surveillance: complaint handling, adverse event reporting, trending, and corrective/preventive action to maintain product quality.

inputs.name: quality-manual
inputs.desc: Quality system procedures for complaint handling and CAPA

inputs.name: control-plan
inputs.desc: Manufacturing controls and inspection specifications

outputs.name: capa-system-records
outputs.desc: CAPA log with root cause analyses, corrective actions, effectiveness checks, and closure records

outputs.name: post-market-surveillance-report
outputs.desc: Trending of complaints, adverse events, and quality metrics with periodic management review

process: Complaint handling: log every complaint with date, device identification, complaint description, and reporter information. Evaluate each complaint for reportability: if the complaint involves death, serious injury, or malfunction that could cause either, file an MDR (Medical Device Report) with FDA within 30 days (5 days for events requiring remedial action).

For each complaint requiring investigation, perform root cause analysis: collect the device for analysis if possible, review production records for the device (lot history, inspection results, any process deviations), and determine whether the issue is a design problem, manufacturing problem, or use problem.

CAPA process: corrective action addresses an existing nonconformity and prevents recurrence. Preventive action addresses a potential nonconformity before it occurs. For each CAPA, document the problem description, investigation, root cause, action plan, implementation, and effectiveness verification.

Effectiveness verification: after implementing a corrective action, monitor the relevant metric for a defined period (typically 3-6 months or 3 production lots) to confirm the problem does not recur. If it does recur, the CAPA is ineffective and must be reopened with a different root cause or action.

Post-market surveillance trending: track complaint rate per units distributed, adverse event rate, return rate, and internal quality metrics (reject rate, CAPA count, audit findings). Report trends to management at defined intervals (quarterly or annually). Increasing trends trigger investigation before they become reportable events.
